subject: Mathematics
title: Priya's Chocolate Cake Party
hook: Priya bakes a cake, cuts it into pieces, and learns fractions and decimals by sharing with friends.

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: bakes cakes and discovers fractions through sharing

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: helps measure recipe ingredients and split portions

slides.title: The Birthday Cake Bake
slides.storyContext: Priya bakes a big chocolate cake for her birthday. She cuts it into 8 equal slices. Arjun eats 2 slices. What fraction did he eat?

points.label: Setup
points.text: One whole cake, 8 equal pieces, Arjun takes 2 pieces

slides.inSimpleWords: Fractions show parts of something whole.

image.alt: The Birthday Cake Bake — Fractions and Decimals

slides.title: Understanding Fractions
slides.storyContext: Priya explains: the bottom number (8) tells you how many equal parts. The top number (2) tells you how many parts Arjun got.

points.label: Numerator (top)
points.text: 2 — the pieces Arjun got

points.label: Denominator (bottom)
points.text: 8 — total equal slices

points.label: Fraction
points.text: 2/8 (two-eighths) of the cake

slides.inSimpleWords: Top = parts taken, bottom = total parts.

image.alt: Understanding Fractions — Fractions and Decimals

slides.title: Fractions in Real Cakes
slides.storyContext: Priya cuts another cake into halves (2 parts). Arjun eats 1 half. She cuts a third cake into quarters (4 parts) and Arjun gets 1 quarter.

example.problem: Name the fractions: 1 half, 1 quarter, 2 halves
example.solution: 1/2 (one-half), 1/4 (one-quarter), 2/2 = 1 whole (two halves)

slides.inSimpleWords: Halves, thirds, quarters are common fractions.

image.alt: Fractions in Real Cakes — Fractions and Decimals

slides.title: Comparing Fractions
slides.storyContext: Priya has 1/4 cake left. Arjun has 1/2 cake left. Who has more?

points.label: Same numerators
points.text: 1/4 vs 1/2 — smaller denominator = bigger piece
Half is bigger than a quarter

points.label: Tip
points.text: Smaller bottom number = bigger actual piece

slides.inSimpleWords: Smaller bottom means a bigger slice.

image.alt: Comparing Fractions — Fractions and Decimals

slides.title: Intro to Decimals
slides.storyContext: Arjun measures milk for the frosting: 0.5 litres (half a litre) and 0.25 litres (a quarter). Decimals use points, not fractions!

points.label: Decimal point
points.text: The dot (.) separates whole from parts
Same as 1/2 (five-tenths)
Same as 1/4 (twenty-five hundredths)
One-tenth of a whole
One-hundredth of a whole

slides.inSimpleWords: Decimals show parts using a point.

image.alt: Intro to Decimals — Fractions and Decimals

slides.title: Fractions and Decimals Together
slides.storyContext: Priya reads a recipe: 3/4 cup sugar (same as 0.75 cup). She uses 1/2 cup flour (same as 0.5 cup). Arjun writes both ways.

example.problem: Write as both fraction and decimal: 3/4, 1/2, 1/10

slides.inSimpleWords: Fractions and decimals are two ways to say the same part.

image.alt: Fractions and Decimals Together — Fractions and Decimals

slides.title: The Cake Sharing Problem
slides.storyContext: Priya bakes 3 cakes. Each has 8 slices. She gives 2/8 to Arjun, 3/8 to a friend, and keeps 1/8. How many slices are left unsold?

points.label: Problem
points.text: Total 24 slices. 2/8 + 3/8 + 1/8 = 6/8. How many remain?

example.problem: 24 slices − (2/8 + 3/8 + 1/8) = ? slices left

slides.inSimpleWords: Add fractions and subtract from the total.

image.alt: The Cake Sharing Problem — Fractions and Decimals

slides.title: The Party Success
slides.storyContext: Priya's birthday party is perfect. Everyone gets a fair share: Arjun gets 1/4, friend gets 1/3, family gets the rest. Fractions made sharing fair and fun!

points.label: Lesson
points.text: Fractions and decimals help us divide, measure, and share wisely in everyday life

slides.inSimpleWords: Fair sharing needs fractions and decimals.

image.alt: The Party Success — Fractions and Decimals

slides.title: Fractions & Decimals Recap
slides.storyContext: Priya and Arjun recap their delicious discovery.

points.label: Fractions
points.text: Top = parts taken, bottom = total parts (e.g., 2/8)

points.label: Common fractions
points.text: 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 3/4 appear everywhere

points.label: Decimals
points.text: Use a point: 0.5, 0.25, 0.75 = same as fractions

points.label: Use it
points.text: Cooking, measuring, sharing, money

slides.inSimpleWords: Fractions and decimals split whole things fairly.

image.alt: Fractions & Decimals Recap — Fractions and Decimals

slides.title: Equivalent Fractions
slides.storyContext: Priya notices: 2/8 cake is the same as 1/4 cake! Same piece, different names. Multiply or divide top and bottom by the same number.

points.label: Equivalent
points.text: 2/8 = 1/4 (both are half of a half)

points.label: How to make
points.text: Multiply or divide numerator AND denominator by the same number

points.label: Example
points.text: 1/2 = 2/4 = 4/8 = 8/16 (all the same piece)

points.label: Simplify
points.text: 6/9 = 2/3 (divide both by 3)

slides.inSimpleWords: Same piece, different numbers = equivalent fractions.

slides.title: Adding and Subtracting Fractions
slides.storyContext: Priya has 1/4 cake. Her friend brings 1/4 cake. Together, how much do they have? Arjun uses the same denominator trick.
slides.inSimpleWords: Add or subtract fractions with the same bottom number easily.

slides.title: Priya's Recipe Scaling
slides.storyContext: Priya wants to make 2 cakes instead of 1. The recipe says 1/2 cup sugar. For 2 cakes, she needs 1/2 × 2 = 1 cup. Multiplying fractions!

points.label: Scenario
points.text: Double the recipe, double each ingredient

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply fractions to scale recipes up or down.

slides.title: Multiplying and Dividing Fractions
slides.storyContext: To multiply: top × top, bottom × bottom. To divide: flip the second fraction and multiply.

points.label: Divide
points.text: 1/2 ÷ 1/4 = 1/2 × 4/1 = 4/2 = 2 (flip the second fraction)

points.label: Real use
points.text: 3/4 × 2 = 6/4 = 1.5 cups (recipe scaling)

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply tops and bottoms; flip to divide.

slides.title: Decimals in Measurement
slides.storyContext: Priya measures: 2.5 litres of milk, 0.75 grams of salt, 1.25 kg of flour. Understanding decimal place values helps her read scales accurately.

example.problem: What is 2.5 in fractions? And 0.75?
example.solution: 2.5 = 2 1/2 (two and one-half). 0.75 = 3/4 (three-quarters)

slides.inSimpleWords: Decimals appear on scales, meters, and measuring tools.

slides.title: Tenths and Hundredths
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks: what's the difference between 0.1 and 0.01? Priya shows: 0.1 is 1/10 (one stripe out of 10). 0.01 is 1/100 (one square out of 100).

points.label: Reading decimals
points.text: 0.37 = thirty-seven hundredths = 37/100

points.label: Tip
points.text: More decimal places = smaller pieces

slides.inSimpleWords: Decimal places show how fine the divisions are.

slides.title: Money and Decimals
slides.storyContext: Priya buys a cake mix for 2.50 rupees, frosting for 0.99 rupees, candles for 1.25 rupees. How much did she spend? Use decimals to add money.

example.solution: 2.50 + 0.99 + 1.25 = 4.74 rupees (line up decimal points when adding)

slides.inSimpleWords: Decimals help us add money and prices.

slides.title: Arjun's Careful Measurements
slides.storyContext: Arjun measures butter: 0.25 kg (1/4 kg). Oil: 0.5 litre (1/2 litre). Baking soda: 0.01 kg (1/100 kg). Tiny fractions and decimals make the cake perfect!

points.label: Precision
points.text: Recipes need exact fractions and decimals

slides.inSimpleWords: Baking teaches us to be precise with fractions.

slides.title: Converting Between Fractions and Decimals
slides.storyContext: Priya writes a fraction conversion chart: 1/2 = 0.5, 1/4 = 0.25, 3/4 = 0.75, 1/5 = 0.2, 1/10 = 0.1.

points.label: How to convert
points.text: Divide numerator by denominator; 3/4 = 3÷4 = 0.75

points.label: Reverse
points.text: 0.75 = 75/100 = 3/4 (simplify by dividing by 25)

slides.inSimpleWords: Divide the top by the bottom to get a decimal.

slides.title: Comparing Decimals
slides.storyContext: Two cakes: one is 0.5 litres of milk, the other is 0.75 litres. Which uses more milk? Arjun lines up decimals to compare: 0.5 < 0.75.

example.problem: Compare: 0.5 vs 0.75, and 0.25 vs 0.2

slides.inSimpleWords: Line up decimals to compare them easily.

slides.title: Mixed Numbers and Improper Fractions
slides.storyContext: Priya has 2 1/2 cakes (two and a half). This is the same as 5/2 cakes (five-halves). Can she convert between them?

example.problem: Convert 2 1/2 to improper fraction, and 7/3 to mixed number

slides.inSimpleWords: Mixed numbers = whole + fraction. Improper = top bigger than bottom.

slides.title: The Baking Challenge
slides.storyContext: Arjun wants to bake 1.5 times the original recipe to feed more guests. Every ingredient needs multiplying: sugar 1/2 cup becomes 0.75 cups. Fractions and decimals save the day!

points.label: Scaling
points.text: 1/2 × 1.5 = 0.75 (three-quarters of the ingredient)

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply fractions and decimals to scale up recipes.

slides.title: Rounding Decimals
slides.storyContext: Priya's kitchen scale shows 0.347 kg of flour, but she rounds to 0.35 kg (nearest hundredth). Rounding makes numbers easier to use.

points.label: Round to tenths
points.text: 0.347 ≈ 0.3 (3 is less than 5, so round down)

points.label: Round to hundredths
points.text: 0.347 ≈ 0.35 (7 is 5 or more, so round up)

points.label: Rule
points.text: Look at the next digit: 5+ round up, less than 5 round down

slides.inSimpleWords: Rounding makes decimals shorter and easier.

slides.title: Percent and Fractions
slides.storyContext: Priya's cake recipe is 50% (half) eggs, 25% (quarter) flour, 25% sugar. Percents are fractions with denominator 100!

example.problem: If a cake is 50% sugar, how much sugar is in 8 kg cake?

slides.inSimpleWords: Percent means out of 100. 50% = 1/2, 25% = 1/4.

slides.title: Real-World Fraction and Decimal Challenge
slides.storyContext: Priya makes 3 cakes: Cake 1 needs 0.5 kg flour, Cake 2 needs 3/4 kg, Cake 3 needs 1.25 kg. Total flour used? Also, if flour costs 0.04 rupees per gram, what's the cost?

example.problem: 0.5 + 0.75 + 1.25 = ? kg. Then cost = answer × 1000 grams × 0.04 = ?

slides.inSimpleWords: Combine fractions, decimals, and money in real problems.

slides.title: Fractions and Decimals Daily
slides.storyContext: Now Priya uses fractions and decimals everywhere: in sports (3/4 of the goal reached), weather (0.8 chance of rain), shopping (25% discount), cooking, and sharing. Math is life!

points.label: Everywhere
points.text: Fractions and decimals appear in every corner of daily life

slides.inSimpleWords: Fractions and decimals are part of everything we do.

slides.title: Fractions & Decimals Mastery
slides.storyContext: Priya and Arjun celebrate their journey from cake slices to complex fraction and decimal problems. They're ready for any real-world challenge!

points.label: Fractions
points.text: Numerator/denominator; 1/2, 1/4, 3/4 are common

points.label: Decimals
points.text: Use point: 0.5, 0.25, 0.75; tenths and hundredths

points.label: Equivalence
points.text: 1/2 = 0.5 = 50%; fractions, decimals, percents = same idea

points.label: Operations
points.text: Add, subtract, multiply, divide; convert between forms

points.label: Use it daily
points.text: Cooking, money, measurements, recipes, shopping

slides.inSimpleWords: Fractions and decimals are everywhere in life!

subject: Mathematics
title: Arjun's Garden Design
hook: Arjun designs a school garden using rectangles, circles, and triangles, then builds 3D structures.

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: plans the garden layout using shapes and angles

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: calculates area and perimeter for planting

slides.title: The Garden Plan
slides.storyContext: The school wants a beautiful garden. Arjun is in charge of design. He uses a big rectangle for the main plot, circles for flower beds, and triangles for shade structures.

points.label: Challenge
points.text: Draw and measure shapes to use space wisely

slides.inSimpleWords: Shapes help plan and build gardens.

image.alt: The Garden Plan — Geometry Shapes

slides.title: 2D Shapes: Sides and Angles
slides.storyContext: Priya teaches Arjun about flat (2D) shapes: a rectangle has 4 sides and 4 right angles (90°). A triangle has 3 sides and 3 angles.

points.label: Rectangle
points.text: 4 sides, 4 right angles (90°), opposite sides equal

points.label: Triangle
points.text: 3 sides, 3 angles, many types (right, equilateral, isosceles)

points.label: Circle
points.text: No sides, no angles, all points same distance from centre

points.label: Square
points.text: Special rectangle: 4 equal sides, 4 right angles

slides.inSimpleWords: Shapes have sides and angles.

image.alt: 2D Shapes: Sides and Angles — Geometry Shapes

slides.title: Calculating Perimeter
slides.storyContext: Arjun's main garden plot is a rectangle: 8 metres long, 5 metres wide. He needs to fence it. How much fencing does he need?

example.problem: Rectangle 8m × 5m. What's the perimeter (distance around)?
example.solution: Perimeter = 2(length + width) = 2(8+5) = 2(13) = 26 metres of fencing needed

slides.inSimpleWords: Perimeter = add all the sides.

image.alt: Calculating Perimeter — Geometry Shapes

slides.title: Calculating Area
slides.storyContext: Priya asks: how much soil do we need for the garden? We measure the AREA (space inside), not just around it.

points.label: Area of rectangle
points.text: length × width = 8 × 5 = 40 square metres

points.label: Area of square
points.text: side × side; for 5m side: 5 × 5 = 25 square metres

points.label: Area of triangle
points.text: 1/2 × base × height

points.label: Square metres
points.text: Unit for measuring area (m²)

slides.inSimpleWords: Area = space inside a shape.

image.alt: Calculating Area — Geometry Shapes

slides.title: Designing Flower Beds
slides.storyContext: Arjun designs three flower bed shapes: a square (4m × 4m), a triangle (base 6m, height 4m), and a circle (radius 3m).

example.problem: Find the areas: Square 4×4, Triangle base 6 height 4, Circle radius 3
example.solution: Square: 4×4=16 m²; Triangle: 1/2×6×4=12 m²; Circle: 3.14×3²≈28 m²

slides.inSimpleWords: Different shapes need different area formulas.

image.alt: Designing Flower Beds — Geometry Shapes

slides.title: 3D Shapes (Objects with Volume)
slides.storyContext: For shade, Arjun plans a small hut. That's a 3D shape! A cube (box), a cone, and a cylinder are common 3D shapes.

points.label: Cube
points.text: 6 square faces, 8 corners, all sides equal (dice shape)

points.label: Cuboid (box)
points.text: 6 rectangular faces, length, width, height differ

points.label: Sphere
points.text: Ball-shaped, no flat faces, no corners

points.label: Cylinder
points.text: Two circular faces, curved surface (tin can shape)

points.label: Cone
points.text: One circular base, one point at top (ice cream cone)

slides.inSimpleWords: 3D shapes have volume (thickness).

image.alt: 3D Shapes (Objects with Volume) — Geometry Shapes

slides.title: The Garden Structure
slides.storyContext: Arjun's shade hut is a cube with 2m sides. He needs to know the volume (how much air inside). What's the volume?

points.label: Problem
points.text: A cube hut: 2m × 2m × 2m. What's the volume?

example.problem: Volume of a cube with 2m sides = ?
example.solution: Volume = side × side × side = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 cubic metres (m³)

slides.inSimpleWords: Volume = space inside 3D shapes.

image.alt: The Garden Structure — Geometry Shapes

slides.title: The Garden Grand Opening
slides.storyContext: The garden is built! A rectangle of soil (40 m²), circle flower beds (28 m²), triangle shade areas, and a cube hut (8 m³). Arjun's geometry design is perfect!

points.label: Success
points.text: Geometry made the garden beautiful, organized, and functional

slides.inSimpleWords: Shapes turn plans into real gardens.

image.alt: The Garden Grand Opening — Geometry Shapes

slides.title: Geometry Mastered
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Priya celebrate their shape skills.

points.label: 2D shapes
points.text: Rectangles, triangles, circles (flat, no thickness)

points.label: Perimeter
points.text: Distance around a shape

points.label: Area
points.text: Space inside a shape (square metres)

points.label: 3D shapes
points.text: Cubes, spheres, cylinders (have volume)

points.label: Use it
points.text: Building, designing, planning, architecture

slides.inSimpleWords: Geometry helps us design and measure our world.

image.alt: Geometry Mastered — Geometry Shapes

slides.title: Types of Triangles
slides.storyContext: Priya shows Arjun three triangle types: equilateral (all sides equal), isosceles (two sides equal), and scalene (all sides different). And right triangles have a 90° angle.

points.label: Equilateral
points.text: All 3 sides equal, all angles 60°

points.label: Isosceles
points.text: 2 sides equal, 2 angles equal

points.label: Scalene
points.text: All sides different, all angles different

points.label: Right triangle
points.text: One 90° angle, used in construction and ramps

slides.inSimpleWords: Triangles come in many shapes and sizes.

slides.title: Perimeter of Different Shapes
slides.storyContext: Arjun calculates fencing for all garden borders: a square plot (5m sides), a circle flower bed (radius 2m), and an equilateral triangle arbor (3m sides).

example.problem: Find perimeters: Square 5m, Circle radius 2m, Triangle 3m sides
example.solution: Square: 4×5 = 20m. Circle: 2πr = 2×3.14×2 ≈ 12.56m. Triangle: 3+3+3 = 9m

slides.inSimpleWords: Each shape has its own perimeter formula.

slides.title: Measuring the Curved Path
slides.storyContext: Arjun plans a circular walking path around the garden. Priya reminds him: circles use π (pi), the magic number that appears everywhere!

points.label: Discovery
points.text: Circumference (around a circle) = 2πr or πd, where r = radius, d = diameter

slides.inSimpleWords: Circles use the special number π (about 3.14).

slides.title: Understanding Angles
slides.storyContext: Arjun learns: angles measure turn, from 0° (no turn) to 360° (full circle). A right angle is 90°. Two right angles = 180° (straight line).

points.label: Right angle
points.text: 90°, like a corner of a square

points.label: Acute
points.text: Less than 90°, sharp angle

points.label: Obtuse
points.text: Between 90° and 180°, wide angle

points.label: Straight
points.text: 180°, a flat line

points.label: Full turn
points.text: 360°, back where you started

slides.inSimpleWords: Angles measure how much you turn.

slides.title: Area of a Circle
slides.storyContext: Priya calculates the area of a circular flower bed with radius 3m. She needs to know how much soil to fill it.

example.problem: Circle with radius 3m. What's the area?

slides.inSimpleWords: Area of circle = π × radius × radius.

slides.title: Surface Area of 3D Shapes
slides.storyContext: Arjun's wooden cube hut (2m × 2m × 2m) needs painting on all 6 faces. How much area does he need to paint?

example.problem: Cube with 2m sides. What's the total surface area (all 6 faces)?
example.solution: Each face = 2 × 2 = 4 m². Total = 6 × 4 = 24 m² to paint

slides.inSimpleWords: Surface area = all the outside faces added together.

slides.title: Priya's Symmetry Discovery
slides.storyContext: Priya notices: many garden shapes are symmetric! A square is symmetric in 4 ways. A circle has infinite symmetry. Symmetry makes gardens beautiful.

points.label: Beauty
points.text: Symmetry appears in nature and design

slides.inSimpleWords: Shapes can look the same from different angles.

slides.title: Coordinates and Grid
slides.storyContext: Arjun uses a grid (like a checkerboard) to plan his garden. Each plant gets coordinates: (row, column). Arjun plants roses at (2,3) and tulips at (5,1).

points.label: Coordinate
points.text: (x, y) = position on a grid

points.label: Origin
points.text: (0, 0) = starting point, bottom-left or top-left

points.label: x-axis
points.text: Horizontal (left-right)

points.label: y-axis
points.text: Vertical (up-down)

slides.inSimpleWords: Coordinates help us locate things on a grid.

slides.title: Plotting Shapes on a Grid
slides.storyContext: Arjun draws a rectangle on his grid using coordinates: corners at (1,1), (1,4), (5,4), and (5,1). He calculates its dimensions.

example.problem: Rectangle corners: (1,1), (1,4), (5,4), (5,1). Length? Width?
example.solution: Length = 5-1 = 4 units. Width = 4-1 = 3 units. Area = 4 × 3 = 12 square units

slides.inSimpleWords: Grids help us draw and measure shapes.

slides.title: Composite Shapes
slides.storyContext: Arjun's garden design is an L-shape: a 8m×5m rectangle PLUS a 3m×2m rectangle attached. What's the total area?

example.problem: L-shaped garden: big rectangle 8×5, small rectangle 3×2 attached. Total area?
example.solution: Big: 8×5 = 40 m². Small: 3×2 = 6 m². Total = 40 + 6 = 46 m²

slides.inSimpleWords: Combine shapes by adding their areas.

slides.title: Geometry in Real Buildings
slides.storyContext: Arjun realizes: architects use geometry for everything! Bridges use triangles (strongest shape). Buildings use rectangles. Domes use circles. Geometry is the language of building!

points.label: Architecture
points.text: Geometry is the backbone of all construction

slides.inSimpleWords: Real buildings are made of geometric shapes.

slides.title: Quadrilaterals: Four-Sided Shapes
slides.storyContext: Arjun discovers: quadrilaterals are all four-sided shapes. Rectangles, squares, parallelograms, trapezoids — each has different properties.

points.label: Rectangle
points.text: Opposite sides equal, all angles 90°

points.label: Square
points.text: All sides equal, all angles 90°

points.label: Parallelogram
points.text: Opposite sides parallel and equal, angles not 90°

points.label: Trapezoid
points.text: One pair of parallel sides

slides.inSimpleWords: Four-sided shapes come in many varieties.

slides.title: Volume of a Cuboid (Box)
slides.storyContext: Arjun stores gardening tools in a rectangular box: 3m long, 2m wide, 1.5m tall. How much volume fits inside?

example.problem: Cuboid 3m × 2m × 1.5m. What is the volume?
example.solution: Volume = length × width × height = 3 × 2 × 1.5 = 9 cubic metres (m³)

slides.inSimpleWords: Volume of a box = length × width × height.

slides.title: The Pathways Pattern
slides.storyContext: Arjun designs walking paths through the garden using different shapes: straight rectangles, curved circles, and diagonal triangles. Patterns make it beautiful!

points.label: Design
points.text: Geometry creates visual harmony and flow

slides.inSimpleWords: Shapes create beautiful patterns.

slides.title: Prisms and Pyramids
slides.storyContext: Priya teaches: a prism has two identical faces (like a triangular prism roof). A pyramid has one base and triangular sides meeting at a point (like the pyramids of Egypt!).

points.label: Triangular prism
points.text: 2 triangle faces, 3 rectangular faces

points.label: Rectangular prism
points.text: A cuboid; 6 rectangular faces

points.label: Pyramid
points.text: One polygonal base, triangular sides meet at apex

points.label: Egyptian pyramid
points.text: Square base with 4 triangular sides

slides.inSimpleWords: Prisms have two identical ends. Pyramids have one base.

slides.title: Volume of Cylinders and Spheres
slides.storyContext: Priya asks: how much water fits in a cylindrical rain barrel (radius 1m, height 2m)? What if it were spherical?

example.problem: Cylinder: radius 1m, height 2m. Volume = ?
example.solution: Volume = πr²h = 3.14 × 1² × 2 = 6.28 m³ (roughly 6 cubic metres of water!)

slides.inSimpleWords: Cylinder volume = π × radius² × height.

slides.title: Geometry Mastery Complete
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Priya's garden is a triumph of geometry: 2D shapes for planning, 3D shapes for structures, angles, area, perimeter, and coordinates all working together!

points.label: 2D shapes
points.text: Rectangles, squares, triangles, circles; each has properties

points.label: Perimeter
points.text: Add all sides; circles use πd or 2πr

points.label: Area
points.text: Length×width for rectangles, 1/2×b×h for triangles, πr² for circles

points.label: 3D shapes
points.text: Cubes, cylinders, cones; volume = length×width×height or formulas

points.label: Real-world use
points.text: Planning, building, designing, measuring land, architecture

slides.inSimpleWords: Geometry is everywhere: shapes, sizes, and space!

subject: Science
title: Arjun's Space Adventure
hook: Arjun and Priya zoom through the solar system and visit each planet to learn about our cosmic neighbourhood.

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: navigator with a star map and endless questions

slides.title: Blast Off to Space!
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Priya hop into a rocket at Earth's south pole. They're heading to explore the eight planets orbiting our Sun.

points.label: Setting
points.text: A spacecraft in orbit, with Earth and the Sun visible below

slides.inSimpleWords: The solar system is our home in space.

image.alt: Blast Off to Space! — The Solar System

slides.title: The Sun: Heart of Our System
slides.storyContext: The Sun is enormous, burning hot, and everything orbits it! Arjun feels the warmth even from this distance.

points.label: The Sun
points.text: A giant ball of burning gas (star), gives light and heat

points.label: Size
points.text: 109 times wider than Earth; we could fit 1.3 million Earths inside!

points.label: Energy
points.text: All life on Earth depends on the Sun's energy

points.label: Age
points.text: About 4.6 billion years old (middle-aged for a star)

slides.inSimpleWords: The Sun is a giant fire ball that rules our system.

image.alt: The Sun: Heart of Our System — The Solar System

slides.title: The Eight Planets
slides.storyContext: Priya points to her star map. There are 8 planets, ordered by distance from the Sun. Mercury is closest and hottest; Neptune is farthest and coldest.

points.label: Close planets
points.text: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars (small, rocky, inner)

points.label: Far planets
points.text: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune (huge, icy or gassy, outer)

points.label: Earth
points.text: Our home! Just right for life (water, air, perfect temperature)

points.label: No Pluto
points.text: Pluto was demoted to a 'dwarf planet' in 2006

slides.inSimpleWords: Eight planets orbit the Sun in order.

image.alt: The Eight Planets — The Solar System

slides.title: Mercury to Mars: The Inner Planets
slides.storyContext: Arjun's ship zooms past the inner rocky planets. Mercury is tiny and scorching (450°C!). Venus is thick with clouds. Earth is perfect. Mars is red and cold.

example.problem: Why is Earth special but Mercury and Venus are not?
example.solution: Earth has liquid water, breathable air, and moderate temperature. Mercury is too hot, Venus's atmosphere crushes everything.

slides.inSimpleWords: Rocky planets near the Sun are too harsh for Earth life.

image.alt: Mercury to Mars: The Inner Planets — The Solar System

slides.title: The Gas Giants: Jupiter and Saturn
slides.storyContext: Priya sees Jupiter, the HUGE gas giant with red storms. Then Saturn, with its beautiful rings made of ice and rock.

example.problem: Jupiter is 11 times wider than Earth. How many Earths fit inside Jupiter?
example.solution: About 1,300 Earths fit inside Jupiter! (volume is 11³ times bigger)

slides.inSimpleWords: Gas giants are enormous, not solid, with many moons.

image.alt: The Gas Giants: Jupiter and Saturn — The Solar System

slides.title: The Moon: Earth's Faithful Friend
slides.storyContext: As they return, Arjun and Priya orbit Earth and marvel at the Moon. It orbits Earth, causes tides, and lights our night sky.

points.label: The Moon
points.text: Earth's natural satellite, orbits us every 27 days

points.label: Tides
points.text: Moon's gravity pulls Earth's oceans, creating high and low tides

points.label: Phases
points.text: New moon, crescent, half moon, full moon (Earth sees different lit parts)

points.label: Distance
points.text: About 384,000 km away (still our nearest neighbour)

slides.inSimpleWords: The Moon dances around Earth every month.

image.alt: The Moon: Earth's Faithful Friend — The Solar System

slides.title: Asteroid Belt Mystery
slides.storyContext: Between Mars and Jupiter, millions of rocks float in an asteroid belt. Priya asks: how did this belt form?

points.label: Challenge
points.text: The asteroid belt might be pieces of a planet that never formed. Why?

example.problem: What might have prevented a planet from forming in the asteroid belt?
example.solution: Jupiter's strong gravity scattered and prevented rocks from clumping together to form a planet.

slides.inSimpleWords: The asteroid belt is cosmic rubble.

image.alt: Asteroid Belt Mystery — The Solar System

slides.title: Home Sweet Earth
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Priya land back on Earth. Looking up at the night sky, they see the Moon and planets they visited. Earth suddenly feels precious and unique.

points.label: Realization
points.text: Our planet is a rare jewel in a vast solar system

slides.inSimpleWords: Earth is special, and we must care for it.

image.alt: Home Sweet Earth — The Solar System

slides.title: The Solar System Recap
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Priya chart their adventure and what they learned.

points.label: The Sun
points.text: Giant star at the centre, gives light and heat

points.label: 8 Planets
points.text: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars (inner rocky); Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune (outer giant)

points.label: The Moon
points.text: Earth's satellite, causes tides, lights the night

points.label: Why Earth?
points.text: Water, air, right temperature = perfect for life

points.label: Explore
points.text: There is so much more to discover in space!

slides.inSimpleWords: The solar system is our cosmic home to explore.

image.alt: The Solar System Recap — The Solar System

slides.title: Orbit and Revolution
slides.storyContext: Priya explains: planets don't just sit still. They orbit (go around) the Sun in elliptical paths. Earth takes 365 days for one full orbit = 1 year!

points.label: Orbit
points.text: Path a planet travels around the Sun

points.label: Ellipse
points.text: Stretched circle, not perfectly round (Kepler's law)

points.label: Year
points.text: Time for one complete orbit around Sun

points.label: Distance matters
points.text: Farther planets take longer (Neptune = 165 Earth years!)

slides.inSimpleWords: Planets dance around the Sun in oval paths.

slides.title: Mercury's Quick Race
slides.storyContext: Arjun visits Mercury, the speedster. It orbits the Sun in just 88 days! Priya explains: closer to the Sun = faster orbit (weaker gravity tug means faster speed needed).

points.label: Mercury fact
points.text: Closest planet, fastest orbit, most extreme temperatures (day: 430°C, night: -170°C)

slides.inSimpleWords: Mercury is the fastest planet.

slides.title: Rotation and Day
slides.storyContext: Arjun learns: rotation is spinning on an axis. Earth spins once every 24 hours = 1 day. But Venus rotates BACKWARDS and takes 243 Earth days to spin once!

points.label: Rotation
points.text: Spin on the planet's own axis

points.label: Day
points.text: Time for one complete rotation

points.label: Earth
points.text: 1 rotation = 24 hours = 1 day

points.label: Venus
points.text: Rotates backwards (retrograde), 243 Earth days per rotation (longer than its year!)

slides.inSimpleWords: Rotation makes days; planets spin at different speeds.

slides.title: Seasons on Earth
slides.storyContext: Priya asks: why do we have summer and winter? Because Earth's axis is tilted 23.5°! When the Northern Hemisphere tilts toward the Sun = summer.

example.problem: If Earth's axis weren't tilted, would we have seasons?
example.solution: No! Seasons happen because the tilt changes how much sunlight hits each hemisphere. No tilt = no seasons, just constant temperature year-round.

slides.inSimpleWords: Earth's tilt gives us seasons.

slides.title: Gravity: The Force Holding Everything
slides.storyContext: Arjun floats in the spaceship and learns: gravity is the invisible force that pulls everything together. It keeps us on Earth, keeps the Moon orbiting Earth, and keeps planets orbiting the Sun.

points.label: Gravity
points.text: Invisible force that attracts all objects

points.label: Mass
points.text: More mass = stronger gravity (Sun's huge mass holds all planets)

points.label: Weight
points.text: Result of gravity pulling on your mass (lighter on Moon than Earth)

points.label: Distance matters
points.text: Gravity gets weaker far away (why outer planets orbit slower)

slides.inSimpleWords: Gravity is the cosmic glue holding the solar system together.

slides.title: Moons of the Planets
slides.storyContext: Arjun discovers: Earth has 1 Moon, Mars has 2, Jupiter has 95+ (the record holder!). Each moon orbits its planet just like planets orbit the Sun.

example.problem: Jupiter's moon Io orbits every 1.77 days. If I measure its orbit, can I calculate Io's distance from Jupiter?
example.solution: Using Kepler's third law, shorter orbital period = closer to the planet. Io is very close (422,000 km) and experiences intense heat from Jupiter's tidal forces.

slides.inSimpleWords: Moons orbit planets just like planets orbit stars.

slides.title: Uranus and Neptune: The Ice Giants
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Priya reach the outer ice giants. Uranus rotates on its side (98° tilt — maybe hit by an asteroid long ago!). Neptune has the fastest winds in the solar system (2,100 km/h).

example.problem: Uranus takes 84 Earth years to orbit the Sun. Neptune takes 165 years. Which is farther from the Sun?
example.solution: Neptune is farther (165 years > 84 years). Distant planets take longer orbits.

slides.inSimpleWords: Outer planets are mysterious and extreme.

slides.title: Priya's Comet Discovery
slides.storyContext: High above the solar system, Priya spots a comet zooming toward the Sun! It has a bright tail made of ice and dust. Comets visit from the far edges of space.

points.label: Comet fact
points.text: Icy rock from the Oort Cloud, tail always points away from the Sun (solar wind pushes it)

slides.inSimpleWords: Comets are icy wanderers from the distant solar system edge.

slides.title: Habitable Zone: The Goldilocks Principle
slides.storyContext: Priya teaches: planets in the habitable zone are just right for life. Not too hot (like Mercury), not too cold (like Neptune). Earth is in the zone, Mars is close but just barely cold.

points.label: Habitable zone
points.text: Region around a star where liquid water can exist

points.label: Too close
points.text: Planet too hot, water boils away

points.label: Too far
points.text: Planet too cold, water freezes

points.label: Just right
points.text: Earth, and potentially Mars (in the past or with terraforming)

slides.inSimpleWords: The habitable zone is where life can thrive.

slides.title: Venus: The Runaway Greenhouse
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks: Venus is similar size to Earth, but why is it a hellscape? Runaway greenhouse effect! CO2 atmosphere, trapped heat, surface temp 462°C.

example.problem: If Venus and Earth are similar sizes, why is Venus 8× hotter?
example.solution: Venus's thick CO2 atmosphere traps heat (greenhouse effect gone wild). A cautionary tale about atmosphere and climate!

slides.inSimpleWords: Venus shows how atmosphere can trap heat dangerously.

slides.title: The Solar System's Size
slides.storyContext: Priya tries to visualize: if the Sun is a marble (1cm), Earth would be 1mm across, 1 meter away. The nearest star (Proxima Centauri) would be 270km away! The solar system is VAST.

example.problem: If Sun = 1cm, Earth is 1mm, 1m away. Where is Neptune (30× farther than Earth)?
example.solution: Neptune would be 30 meters away! And Pluto 40m away. The solar system is mostly empty space.

slides.inSimpleWords: The solar system is enormous compared to what we see.

slides.title: The Future of Our Solar System
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Priya learn: in 5 billion years, the Sun will swell and swallow Mercury, Venus, and Earth. But not today! We have time to explore and protect our home.

points.label: Red Giant phase
points.text: Sun's future when it runs out of hydrogen fuel

slides.inSimpleWords: Even the Sun has a life cycle, but ours lasts billions of years.

slides.title: Outer Planets' Rings and Storms
slides.storyContext: Priya explains: Saturn's famous rings are ice and rock. But did you know Jupiter, Uranus, and Neptune have rings too? And Jupiter has a Great Red Spot — a storm bigger than Earth!

points.label: Saturn's rings
points.text: Most visible, made of billions of ice particles

points.label: Jupiter's Great Red Spot
points.text: Storm larger than Earth, raging for 300+ years

points.label: Ring formation
points.text: Moons broken apart by gravity, or leftover from solar system formation

slides.inSimpleWords: Giant planets have spectacular rings and storms.

slides.title: Rocky vs Gas Planets
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Priya compare: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars are small, solid, and dense. Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune are huge, gaseous, and light for their size!

example.problem: Mercury is 1/400th the mass of Earth. Jupiter is 318× Earth's mass. Why do we split planets this way?
example.solution: Composition determines everything: rocky planets formed closer to the hot Sun (metals, rock survive). Gas giants formed farther out where hydrogen and helium were captured.

slides.inSimpleWords: Near the Sun = rocky. Far from Sun = gassy.

slides.title: Meteors, Meteorites, and Meteoroids
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Priya learn the difference: meteoroids are space rocks, meteors are meteoroids burning in Earths atmosphere (shooting stars!), and meteorites are the ones that land on Earth.

points.label: Meteoroid
points.text: Rock in space

points.label: Meteor
points.text: Meteoroid burning in atmosphere (shooting star)

points.label: Meteorite
points.text: Meteor that lands on Earth

points.label: Impact
points.text: Large meteorite can create craters

slides.inSimpleWords: Space rocks have different names depending on where they are.

slides.title: Wonder and Discovery
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Priya finish their adventure amazed at the solar systems complexity: billions of objects, incredible distances, and Earth — our perfect home. Science makes it all understandable!

points.label: Inspiration
points.text: The solar system inspires us to explore and protect our world

slides.inSimpleWords: The solar system is vast, beautiful, and worth exploring.

slides.title: The Solar System Mastered
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Priya's incredible journey complete. They've explored 8 planets, understood orbits, rotation, gravity, moons, and what makes Earth special.

points.label: The Sun
points.text: Central star, 4.6 billion years old, powers all life

points.label: Planets
points.text: 8 planets orbit in ellipses; inner rocky, outer giant/ice

points.label: Moons & objects
points.text: 95+ moons, asteroid belt, comets, dwarf planets

points.label: Motion
points.text: Orbit (around Sun) + rotation (on axis); gravity keeps it all together

points.label: Earth's place
points.text: Rare habitable zone, perfect conditions for life, our only home

slides.inSimpleWords: The solar system is our cosmic backyard, endlessly fascinating!
